summary: A revision of the Mail Box Protocol by the file transfer committee. Mail is limited to ASCII text formatted for a line printer, a new FTP command called Append With Create is added, and a standard mailbox path name is defined. It replaces RFC 221.

eli5.summary: The plan for dropping notes into a computer's mailbox was tidied up: only plain text, and a new command that makes the mailbox if it does not exist.

questions: how did early arpanet mail to printers work
subtitle: A 1971 revision of the Mail Box Protocol, which sends plain text mail to a line printer using FTP.

tldr.problem: ARPANET hosts needed a simple way to deliver text mail to a person or printer on another host.
tldr.mechanism: A mail item is sent as a file with the FTP Append With Create request to socket 3, using network ASCII formatted for a printer with a 72 character line and a 66 line page, under a standard mailbox path name.
tldr.outcome: The revision limits mail to ASCII text for a line printer, adds Append With Create to FTP, and replaces RFC 221.

today: RFC 278 replaces RFC 221 and relies on the File Transfer Protocol of its time. Its metadata does not record it as obsoleted.

sections.title: What Changed
sections.content:
The file transfer committee met and confirmed the usefulness of the Mail Box Protocol of RFC 221. Three changes were made. Mail is only ASCII strings of text formatted for a network standard line printer. A new File Transfer Protocol command, Append With Create, appends to a file if it exists and creates it if it does not. And the standard mailbox path name is now "MAIL" <separator> ("PRINTER"/<ident>), where the separator is the ASCII GS character, octal 035.

With PRINTER, the receiving site appends to a bulk mail file to be printed or sends it straight to a printer. With a NIC IDENT, it either treats it as PRINTER or appends to a file for that person.
sections.eli5: Mail is now only plain printable text, there is a new command that makes the mailbox if needed, and the mailbox has a standard name.

sections.title: Sending a Mail Item
sections.content:
The protocol uses the Network Control Program, the Initial Connection Protocol, the Data Transfer Protocol and the File Transfer Protocol. The sender connects to standard File Transfer socket 3 and sends the mail item as a file. The only basic operation required is Append With Create, followed by the data, an end-of-file indication and the server's acknowledge.

Transmission is network ASCII. The standard printer has a 72 character line and a 66 line page, and a form feed (hex 0C) moves to a new page. Sending more than that is the sender's responsibility, and the receiving site may handle overruns as it sees fit. The message begins with two copies of an address string, each ended by a form feed, giving the sender's and receiver's names and addresses so a clerk can read and distribute it.
sections.eli5: You knock on door 3, say 'add this note', send the text, and get a thank-you. The first page has the address written twice so a clerk can read it easily.

sections.title: Printer Controls and TIPs
sections.content:
A change-printer-settings control transaction, opcode hex 5A, lets the sender set the line width to 72 characters, use the full printer width, set the page size to 66 lines or set it to infinite. Other control codes can be added later, and all error codes of FTP may be returned.

TIPs then supported only Telnet. People wanting to mail a TIP with a printer could open a standard published socket and send with Telnet. The NIC did not plan automatic network delivery to TIPs, and mail for TIP users goes to their initial file at the NIC.
sections.eli5: The sender can tell the printer how wide or long the pages are. Some small terminals could not take mail directly, so their mail waits at the information office.

references.text: Mail Box Protocol, RFC 221 (NIC 7612), which this RFC revises.
Telnet Protocol, RFC 158 (NIC 6768), cited for the new line convention.
